$$
{P}_{5}(x)=6+12(x-1)+9(x-1)^{2}+4(x-1)^{3}+\frac{5}{4}(x-1)^{4}+\frac{3}{10}(x-1)^{5}.
$$

What is ${f}^{(5)}(1)?$

${f}^{(5)}(1)=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The coefficient of $(x-1)^{5}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{(5)}(1)}{5!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{(5)}(1)}{5!} & =\frac{3}{10} \\ \frac{{f}^{(5)}(1)}{120} & =\frac{3}{10} \\ {f}^{(5)}(1) & =36.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-448b4c89-4022-50f5-af1b-27d8086bba6c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-448b4c89-4022-50f5-af1b-27d8086bba6c" :answer-field/id #uuid "448b4c89-4022-50f5-af1b-27d8086bba6c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-2650b1f4-0b37-597f-9c58-6fa55b3f1254" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2650b1f4-0b37-597f-9c58-6fa55b3f1254"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2650b1f4-0b37-597f-9c58-6fa55b3f1254" :answer/id #uuid "2650b1f4-0b37-597f-9c58-6fa55b3f1254" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "36" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088155 :question/problem "A  linear transformation $T$ represents a dilation. Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}48 \\ -6\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}48 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =6v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=6v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=6.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1235c3ee-01a6-5118-9232-ffc94935dca5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ about $x=0$ is" :question/worked-solution "To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!} \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡0=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡0=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =0+2\cdot x+0\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+(-8)\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =2x-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ee929d99-8395-520f-9fff-986b822a2550"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Given that $v=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1\end{aligned}]$ and $T(v)=[\begin{aligned}48 \\ -6\end{aligned}],$ what is the standard matrix of $T?$"] [17592186088155 :question/worked-solution "We can write $T(v)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(v) & =[\begin{aligned}48 \\ -6\end{aligned}] \\  & =6\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =6v\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $T(v)=6v,$ and so the linear transformation $T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k=6.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the standard matrix of $T$ is

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$"] [17592186088155 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1235c3ee-01a6-5118-9232-ffc94935dca5" :answer-field/id #uuid "1235c3ee-01a6-5118-9232-ffc94935dca5"] $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ about $x=0$ is"] ["question-ca3460ff-fc6a-5037-a239-c26e4d66f531" :question/worked-solution "To find the third-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=0,$ we plug $a=0$ into the general formula to give

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!} \\  & =f(0)+{f}^{′}(0)x+{f}^{″}(0)\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{f}^{‴}(0)\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We need to compute $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & f(0) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}(0) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡0=2 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}(0) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡0=0 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}(0) & =-8\operatorname{cos}⁡0=-8\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we plug the results for $f(0),$ ${f}^{′}(0),$ ${f}^{″}(0),$ and ${f}^{‴}(0)$ into our third-degree Taylor polynomial. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{3}(x) & =0+2\cdot x+0\cdot \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+(-8)\cdot \frac{{x}^{3}}{6} \\  & =2x-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ca3460ff-fc6a-5037-a239-c26e4d66f531" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-ee929d99-8395-520f-9fff-986b822a2550" :answer-field/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Let $I=N$ and ${S}_{i}=[0,\,1+\frac{1}{i}],$ then ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}=$" :question/worked-solution "The union of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\in U\,:\,x\in {A}_{i}\,\,\text{for at least one }{A}_{i},\,\,i\in I}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

Let's now write down a few instances of our indexed sets:

- if $i=1,$ we have ${S}_{1}=[0,2]$

- if $i=2,$ we have ${S}_{2}=[0,\frac{3}{2}]$

- if $i=3,$ we have ${S}_{3}=[0,\frac{4}{3}]$

and so on. 

Notice that as $i$ increases, 

- the left endpoint of the intervals is $0$ for all the sets,

- the right endpoint of the intervals approaches $1$ but never reaches it.

Moreover, all the intervals are contained in ${S}_{1}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}={S}_{1}=[0,2].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284721 :question/id #uuid "13b883ee-4025-5aac-b6bf-58be4872fe51" :question/math-academy-id "q-174454"} {:db/id 17592186287878 :question/id #uuid that the projection of $a$ onto $b$ is the zero vector, find the value of $x.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $a$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $b$ equals the zero vector only when the vectors are perpendicular. 

So, we must have

$$
a⊥b\,⟹\,a\cdot b=0.
$$

Computing the dot product, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & ={a}_{x}\cdot {b}_{x}+{a}_{y}\cdot {b}_{y}+{a}_{z}\cdot {b}_{z} \\  & =-5\cdot x+(-3)\cdot (-2)+1\cdot (-3) \\  & =3-5x.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the dot product equal to $0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot b & =0 \\ 3-5x & =0 \\ -5x & =-3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186290296 :question/id #uuid "cbcf41af-6f81-5a46-9b85-441a34ac9cb2" :question/math-academy-id "q-212459"} {:db/id 17592186290297 :question/id #uuid {{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "For large negative values of $x,$ we have $|8x-7|=-(8x-7).$ Consequently, for $x\to -\infty ,$ we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{|8x-7|}{-5x+2}={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(8x-7)}{-5x+2}.
$$

The horizontal asymptote for $x<0$ is $y={lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(8x-7)}{-5x+2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(\frac{8x}{x}-\frac{7}{x})}{(\frac{-5x}{x}+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-(8-\frac{7}{x})}{(-5+\frac{2}{x})} \\  & =\frac{-(8-0)}{-5+0} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{8}{5}.$"} {:db/id 17592186297272 :question/id #uuid "f75bce11-338e-5172-9aa9-a70e3ac0a182" :question/math-academy-id "q-302242"} {:db/id 17592186314805 :question/worked-solution "The complement of $S,$ denoted $\overset{―}{S},$ consists of every element in the universal set $U$ that is not in the set $S.$

The only elements of $U$ that are not in $S$ are $p,$ $r,$ and $u.$

Therefore, the complement of $S$ is

$$
\overset{―}{S}={p,r,u}.

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Given that ${\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=p,$ express the value of ${\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x$ in terms of $p.$

${\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x),$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x).$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & ={e}^{|-x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={e}^{|x|}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) \\  & =-{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x+p & =0 \\ {\int }_{-2}^{0}{e}^{|x|}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =-p.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186381125 :question/id #uuid "5a7a58f2-bd10-5f94-9790-fc49e15d4c8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-156179"} {:db/id 17592186381132 :question/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055877 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056003 :tutorial/content "Interesting mathematical problems often involve a large (or infinite) collection of sets. Labeling each set with a subscript is often convenient in such situations. 

For example, suppose we define a collection of sets $A_i$ for $i\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N$ as follows:

$$
A_1 = \{1,2\}, \qquad A_2 = \{3,4\}, \qquad A_3 = \{5,6\}, \qquad \ldots
$$

Note the following:

- This collection of $A_i$'s, which we denote $\big\{ A_i \big\}_{i \in \mathbb N},$ is called a **family of indexed sets.**

- The set $i=\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N$ is called the **index set**.

Writing each set with a subscript makes talking about a general $A_i$ easier. In this particular case, for example, we can express a general member of this family in terms of its index:

$$
A_i = \{2i-1,\, 2i\}, \qquad i\in\mathbb N
$$

So, if we wanted to write down the elements of $A_{100},$ we substitute $i=100$ into the definition of $A_i{:}$

$$
A_{100} = \big\{2(100)-1,\, 2(100)\big\} = \{199,200\}
$$

We can use any index set when defining a family of indexed sets. 

For example, consider the indexed family $\big\{ B_x \big\}_{x \in \mathbb R},$ where $B_x$ is the real interval defined by

$$
B_x = \big[ 0, x^2 \big), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Here, the index set is $\mathbb{R}.$ 

To write down, say, the elements of $B_{\color{blue}\sqrt{5}},$ we substitute $x={\color{blue}\sqrt{5}}$ into our definition of $B_x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}_{\sqrt{5}} & =[0,\,(\sqrt{5})^{2}) \\  & =[0,5)\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "94ce30ce-17fc-5813-9947-89a8d392343b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7957 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9a6cdf07-394b-572b-b1c9-fc2d60400ed0" :step/math-academy-id 70625 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055878}} {:db/id 17592186055878 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054831 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054362 :question/id #uuid "154d4cf7-a72a-51b1-bbb3-9bcf83b88e98" :question/math-academy-id "e-12665"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3f986c29-111e-5cb3-8104-62ab734f1c47" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055046} {:db/id 17592186055047} {:db/id 17592186055048} {:db/id 17592186284702} {:db/id 17592186284703} {:db/id 17592186284704} {:db/id 17592186284705} {:db/id 17592186284706}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Elements of an Indexed Family"} :step/id #uuid "0b2b9b72-b07b-51b4-970f-a98643e205c5" :step/math-academy-id 70626 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055879}} {:db/id 17592186055879 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056033 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the indexed family $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ where $I$ is an index set. 

The **union** of a family of indexed sets is the set containing all elements belonging to *at least one* set in the indexed family:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for at least one } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

For example, suppose we have the following family of indexed sets:

$$
X_i = \{ -i, \,0, \, i \}, \qquad i\in \mathbb N
$$

We wish to calculate the following union:

$$
\bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i
$$

To calculate our union, let's write down a few of our indexed sets:

- If $i=1,$ we have $X_1 = \{ -1, 0, 1 \}.$

- If $i=2,$ we have $X_2 = \{ -2, 0, 2 \}.$

- If $i=3,$ we have $X_3 = \{ -3, 0, 3 \}.$

- $\cdots$

and so on. 

Now, note the following:

- It's clear that the $X_i$'s contain only integers. Therefore, any union of $X_i$'s will contain only integers. So, 

$$
\bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i  \subseteq \mathbb Z.
$$

- Notice that *any* integer $n$ belongs to our union. For instance, $n \in \mathbb{N}$ lies in $X_n=\{ -n, 0, n \}$ and, consequently, lies in the union of all $X_i$'s. Therefore, 

$$
\bigcup_{i \in \mathbb N} X_i  \supseteq \mathbb Z.
$$

Thus, using the fact that $A\subseteq B$ and $B\subseteq A$ if and only if $A=B,$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i\in N}{X}_{i} & =\overset{{X}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{{-1,0,1}}}\cup \overset{{X}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{{-2,0,2}}}\cup \overset{{X}_{3}}{\overset{⏞}{{-3,0,3}}}\cup ⋯=Z\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since our index set $I = \mathbb N$ in this example, we can also use the following notation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋃}_{i=1}^{\infty }{X}_{i}=Z\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "44240f43-3346-5c5f-9955-317e4e8ad24c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8177 :tutorial/title "Unions of Indexed  Families"} :step/id #uuid "2ec1fad8-799b-53d9-878f-444b40b1e568" :step/math-academy-id 70630 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055880}} {:db/id 17592186055880 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056034 :tutorial/content "Similarly, the **intersection** of a family of indexed sets $\{A_i\}_{i\in I}$ contains all elements that belong to *all* sets in our family:

$$
\bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \big\{ x\in U \: : \: x \in A_i \:\:\textrm{for all } A_i,\:\: i \in I \big\}
$$

where $U$ is a universal set.

For example, suppose we have the following family of indexed sets:

$$
S_i = \left[ 0, \: 10^{-i} \right], \qquad i \in \mathbb{N}
$$

We wish to compute the following intersection:

$$
\bigcap_{i \in \mathbb{N}} S_i
$$

To calculate our intersection, let's write down a few of our indexed sets:

- If $i=1,$ we have $S_1 = [0, 0.1]$

- If $i=2,$ we have $S_2 = \left[ 0, 0.01 \right]$

- If $i=3,$ we have $S_3 = \left[ 0, 0.001 \right]$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

Now, note the following:

- As $i$ increases, the right endpoint of $S_i$ approaches $0$ but never reaches it.

- The left endpoint equals zero for each $S_i.$

So, the only element that lies in all sets is $0.$ Therefore, the intersection of our indexed family is the set containing zero only:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i\in N}{S}_{i}={0}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since our index set $I = \mathbb N$ in this example, we can also use the following notation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{⋂}_{i=1}^{\infty }{S}_{i}={0}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "03cd6876-c452-576d-8f1a-24bb0fe077ea" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8178 :tutorial/title "Intersections of Indexed  Families"} :step/id #uuid "253c7481-555b-5d32-a3f7-49642ec94a10" 17592186088554 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088904 :tutorial/content "We can draw a curve by defining a relationship between $x$ and $y$ using a third parameter $t.$ For example, suppose we have 

$$
x=2t, \,\,\, y=t^2, \quad -3\leq t\leq 3.
$$

These are the **parametric equations** of the curve.

First, let's create a table for some values of $t\mathbin{:}$

| **$t$** | $-3$ | $-2$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x= 2t$ | $-6$ | $-4$ | $-2$ | $0$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ |
| $y=t^2$ | $9$ | $4$ | $1$ | $0$ | $1$ | $4$ | $9$ |

Plotting these points, we get the following curve:

![](images/f7/f716e12c79731f363ace05965809bfc1963a6c3a231e1c4a96eaf3dbb62c848e.png)

The curve is actually a parabola.
A curve defined by parametric equations is called a **parametric curve** and is said to be "defined parametrically"." :tutorial/id #uuid "f1327a56-c215-50cb-a30e-e43369078a3c" $$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}]
$$

For example, let 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 be the matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}.$ This transformation is a dilation of scale factor $2.$

To visualize the dilation $\mathbf{T},$ consider the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square $\mathrm{R}$ spanned by the vectors, as shown below. 

![](images/6e/6e38185922e9cad6d3961e7c5e755eabf4c52eafd1cc81a1e81a383b4df5ae82.png)

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =Ti=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=2i, \\ {j}^{'} & =Tj=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=2j.\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf{T}$ multiplies vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ by $2.$ The resulting vectors span a larger region, shown below.

![](images/cc/cc6677c641a2a713e0324db90edfdd86a5ca1c096c0ffd70f1216119f36da645.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "689fa0a7-c69e-5bd3-8a10-31aca7d9871f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3536 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b3147c60-fe22-5922-b00c-9f4e25a56724" :step/math-academy-id 20028 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088612}} {:db/id 17592186088610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088931 :tutorial/content "A **reflection in the $x$-axis** is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

To visualize a reflection in the $x$-axis, consider the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square $\mathrm{R}$ spanned by the vectors, as shown below. 

![](images/9e/9e322e6ed1ddb8f1d094633e931cd179b7eb9d6f47acd7c7d0809f113df91b22.png)

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we obtain the following image:

![](images/b9/b93bb91dae85a3e3b40a8d0ade3d4f420064aaa6926431fa7f664c977bb8fd59.png)

Similarly, a **reflection in the $y$-axis** is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Again, we can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-i \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=j\end{aligned}
$$

:step/next {:db/id 17592186088610}} {:db/id 17592186088665 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088956 :tutorial/content "A **reflection in line $y=x$** is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=j \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we obtain the following image:

![](images/0e/0e37a258ea833a2d490fc34a34af40a5c7a18f7589f107c6d0ed631b331c8f2a.png)

Similarly, a **reflection in line $y=-x$** is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we obtain the following image:

![](images/4a/4a83673a409fd2e5d33b0b5f743f57af08cfb27c38e312a636179102c2172b04.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9b34a369-035e-5610-a337-6169ea364331" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4161 :tutorial/title "Reflection in the Lines y=x and y=-x"} :step/id #uuid "0aa5472d-88af-57aa-8bf3-c32dc3b082a4" :step/math-academy-id 25326 :step/next {:db/id 17592186088611}}] :activity/title "Dilations and Reflections as Linear Transformations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186087934} {:db/id 17592186088609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186088930 :tutorial/content "A **dilation** of scale factor $k$ with the center at the origin is a linear transformation that multiplies the standard basis vectors by $k.$ It is represented by the matrix

$$
[\begin{aligned}k & 0 \\ 0 & k\end{aligned}]
$$

For example, let 

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

 be the matrix of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}.$ This transformation is a dilation of scale factor $2.$

To visualize the dilation $\mathbf{T},$ consider the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square $\mathrm{R}$ spanned by the vectors, as shown below. 

![](images/6e/6e38185922e9cad6d3961e7c5e755eabf4c52eafd1cc81a1e81a383b4df5ae82.png)

We can find the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =Ti=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=2i, \\ {j}^{'} & =Tj=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=2j.\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf{T}$ multiplies vectors $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ by $2.$ The resulting vectors span a larger region, shown below.

[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{'} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j \\ {j}^{'} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we obtain the following image:

![](images/4a/4a83673a409fd2e5d33b0b5f743f57af08cfb27c38e312a636179102c2172b04.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "9b34a369-035e-5610-a337-6169ea364331" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4161 :tutorial/title "Reflection in the Lines y=x and y=-x"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186101773} :activity/id #uuid "3a501856-bb65-504b-98d5-6f50a4cbac72" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050866 :topic/id #uuid "6c8df600-6486-5dca-8ab7-e48984c51ac1" :topic/math-academy-id 1222} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186101773 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101923 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can approximate a function $f(x)$ using a second-degree Taylor polynomial. To get this second-degree Taylor polynomial, we add a second term to the linear approximation:

$$
P_2(x) =  \underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}_{\text{linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{new quadratic term}}.
$$

As it turns out, we can keep on adding more and more terms, each time getting better and better approximations. The **third-degree Taylor polynomial** approximation to $f(x),$ denoted $P_3(x),$ is given by

$$
P_3(x) =  \underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \dfrac{1}{2!}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\text{quadratic approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{3!}f^{(3)}(a)(x-a)^3}_{\text{new cubic term}}.
$$

Note that $f^{(3)}$ represents the third derivative of $f.$ In other words, $f^{(3)} = f'''.$

In general, $P_3(x)$ is a better approximation to $f(x)$ compared to $P_2(x),$ provided that $x$ is close to $a.$

**Note:** The phrase "Taylor polynomial" refers to a polynomial that's used to approximate a function.

- The first-degree Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation.

- The second-degree Taylor polynomial is the quadratic approximation.

- The third-degree Taylor polynomial is the cubic approximation." :tutorial/id #uuid "cd509947-98be-52f7-907d-c56ae5e21b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1286 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186101074} {:db/id 17592186101773 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101923 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can approximate a function $f(x)$ using a second-degree Taylor polynomial. To get this second-degree Taylor polynomial, we add a second term to the linear approximation:

$$
P_2(x) =  \underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}_{\text{linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{new quadratic term}}.
$$

As it turns out, we can keep on adding more and more terms, each time getting better and better approximations. The **third-degree Taylor polynomial** approximation to $f(x),$ denoted $P_3(x),$ is given by

$$
P_3(x) =  \underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \dfrac{1}{2!}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\text{quadratic approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{3!}f^{(3)}(a)(x-a)^3}_{\text{new cubic term}}.
$$

Note that $f^{(3)}$ represents the third derivative of $f.$ In other words, $f^{(3)} = f'''.$

In general, $P_3(x)$ is a better approximation to $f(x)$ compared to $P_2(x),$ provided that $x$ is close to $a.$

**Note:** The phrase "Taylor polynomial" refers to a polynomial that's used to approximate a function.

- The first-degree Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation.

- The second-degree Taylor polynomial is the quadratic approximation.

- The third-degree Taylor polynomial is the cubic approximation." :tutorial/id #uuid "cd509947-98be-52f7-907d-c56ae5e21b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1286 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6748e937-6bc9-5c58-a2e7-78aa6b328dd2" :step/math-academy-id 2529 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101781}} {:db/id 17592186101923 :tutorial/content "Recall that we can approximate a function $f(x)$ using a second-degree Taylor polynomial. :topic/math-academy-id 1295} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

For example, consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ shown below. Suppose we know that $|\mathbf{a}|=2,$ $|\mathbf{b}|=3,$ and the angle between the vectors is $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

![](images/a2/a28278cf12885ab7f845407ac2fa7f4ffa00dbe30849a3f8ff41f02e134ed3a0.png)

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

![](images/f0/f0b267fb009e79eb16f86be42edc2c835808b28aa3eaf1c7e857300224ee01ec.png)

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

First, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5962a19e-bb12-54d8-b53a-24578711fa53" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "26031206-512a-5b41-90d5-299987889655" :step/math-academy-id 121755 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106650}} {:db/id 17592186106563 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105701 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105478 :question/id #uuid "3278333b-a29e-54c5-bc94-b5525bc6f751" :question/math-academy-id "e-14617"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "7c9317eb-d1ce-5f42-b69b-a37e643b865b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049360} {:db/id 17592186049653}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106111} {:db/id 17592186106480} {:db/id 17592186287856} {:db/id 17592186287939} {:db/id 17592186292817} {:db/id 17592186292818} {:db/id 17592186297479} {:db/id 17592186297480} {:db/id 17592186339000} {:db/id 17592186339001} {:db/id 17592186339002}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Vector Projection Using Angle and Magnitude"} :step/id #uuid "e6fd410f-37e5-5a4e-a29d-c160c7d2a397" :step/math-academy-id 121756 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106564}} {:db/id 17592186106564 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "146819e4-ecad-5e47-8884-a05b59624d07" :step/math-academy-id 121763} {:db/id 17592186106567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107168 :tutorial/content "Notice that if two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are perpendicular, then by projecting $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ (or $\mathbf{b}$ onto $\mathbf{a}$), we obtain the zero vector.

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

![](images/91/9163eda36b752f1e36195b8b5a1d40bf545ec21a3988f5480d6ddcbb926c00ea.png)

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

> *If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "97117437-4034-5cb8-84a6-675d75d4f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9059 :tutorial/title "Projecting Perpendicular Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "ec38d18e-577a-5ebc-8349-60991ef75b80" :step/math-academy-id 121766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106566}} {:db/id 17592186106650 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} :step/id #uuid "fdc39c18-bf51-5a32-a828-404d1e341f7a" :step/math-academy-id 187844 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106563}}] :activity/title "Calculating a Vector Projection" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105967} {:db/id 17592186106562 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107166 :tutorial/content "The **vector projection** of a vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto another vector $\mathbf{b}$ is the portion that the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends along $\mathbf{b}.$

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} =\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{u}
$$

However, we can write an alternative formula using the formula for the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the original formula for the vector projection, and also substituting $\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{| \, \mathbf{b} \, |},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|}\cdot \frac{b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,{|}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, another general formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e4098700-6d5c-5618-90a8-8dea2d4dbed0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9052 :tutorial/title "A General Formula"} :step/id #uuid "a78e2420-8af1-50c7-9a19-b4ceac9bcde4" :step/math-academy-id 121759 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106565}} {:db/id 17592186107167 :tutorial/content "We have been using the following formula for the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

For example, the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto a perpendicular vector $\mathbf{b}$ looks as follows:

Furthermore, we have the following fact:

> *If $\mathbf{a}$ is a nonzero vector, its projection onto another nonzero vector $\mathbf{b}$ equals the zero vector if and only if the vectors are perpendicular.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "97117437-4034-5cb8-84a6-675d75d4f874" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9059 :tutorial/title "Projecting Perpendicular Vectors"} {:db/id 17592186107181 :tutorial/content "When finding the projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b},$ we sometimes find that the resulting projection vector points in the opposite direction to $\mathbf{b}.$ This happens when the vector $\mathbf{a}$ extends in the direction opposite to that of $\mathbf{b}.$

![](images/0e/0e973e6f6484a9aad863ebfe89fc1ea6356d6a50844931306c6aa2b63be18a8a.png)

Consider two vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b},$ where it is known that 

$$
|\,\mathbf{a}\,|=2,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=3,\qquad \theta = 135^\circ.
$$

Let's calculate $\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a}.$ 

First, notice that the angle between $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ is obtuse. This means we expect the projection vector to point in the opposite direction to that of $\mathbf b.$

Next, we compute the scalar projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}({135}^{∘}) \\  & =2\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the scalar projection is negative. 

Then, we find the unit vector that is parallel to $\mathbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}
$$

Therefore, the vector projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{3}b \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}b.\end{aligned}
$$

This vector points in the direction opposite to $\mathbf{b},$ as expected." :tutorial/id #uuid "2df5fde5-316c-5962-8f0d-56362287c447" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9677 :tutorial/title "The Direction of the Projection Vector"} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186125668} :activity/id #uuid "55d83791-4999-5136-909d-35e46a8ed919" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050004 :topic/id #uuid "25876b80-efb1-53ed-9327-08d34c32cc9a" :topic/math-academy-id 1903} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125668 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125743 :tutorial/content "To calculate the limit at infinity of a rational function, such as

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \infty}\left(\dfrac{x^4}{x^5-x^2}\right),
$$

 we apply the following procedure:

**Step 1:** Divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the *denominator*.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}-{x}^{2}}) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{{x}^{4}÷{x}^{5}}{({x}^{5}-{x}^{2})÷{x}^{5}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}}}{\frac{{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{5}}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{\frac{1}{x}}{1-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}})\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Apply the rule that if $n$ is any positive integer then $\displaystyle \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow \infty}\left(\dfrac{1}{x^n}\right)=0.$ Evaluate the remaining expression to obtain the answer.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{{x}^{4}}{{x}^{5}-{x}^{2}}) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }(\frac{\frac{1}{x}}{1-\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}}) \\  & =\frac{0}{1-0} \\  & =\frac{0}{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ed558480-81a6-5baf-ab3a-f19468f77d72" :tutorial/math-academy-id 258 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "6cb8d91a-6de6-5bd6-878e-78ec12b7fedf" :step/math-academy-id For example, if the universal set is $U = \{ a, b, c, d \},$ then the objects that we can consider are the letters $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and $d.$

- One that we *cannot* consider is $\{ 1, 2, 3 \}.$ We do *not* consider this set because its elements are *not* taken from the universal set. $\quad\color{red}\times$

**complement** of $S,$ denoted $\overline{S},$ consists of every element in $U$ that is **not** in the set $S.$

For example, consider the set $S = \{ 2, 5\}$ in the universe $U = \{ 1,2,3,4,5 \}.$ We can represent these sets using a Venn diagram, as follows:

![](images/20/20726b35619c1b04803c18c8fe12f52db8f07faebca45f64a86c17f8f7077d09.png)

The complement of $S,$ denoted $\overline S,$ consists of all the elements in $U$ that are not in $S.$ To represent $\overline S,$ we will shade in all the area of $U$ that is *outside* of $S,$ as follows:

![](images/c7/c7b25f22a1f70135d09886db58be3646604a861e62d34978a3563343fcd7b298.png)

The elements in the shaded area are $1,$ $3,$ and $4.$ These are the elements of $U$ that are not in $S.$ Therefore, the complement of $S$ is

$$
\overline{S} = \{ 1,3,4 \}.
$$

Also, note that there are several ways to denote the complement of a set. The complement of a set $S$ can be denoted as $\overline{S},$ or $S^c,$ or $S'.$ Here, we will use the convention $\overline{S}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e80b18cd-6881-563b-a21e-aca78742ce9d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4336 :tutorial/title "The Complement of a Set"} :step/id #uuid "854a2440-ad18-5582-be3b-b439bdd69c76" :step/math-academy-id 26377 :step/next {:db/id 17592186158118}} {:db/id 17592186158126 :step/content {:db/id 17592186158477 :tutorial/content "Although Venn diagrams can be useful to visualize complements, we do not have to draw a Venn diagram every time we wish to compute a complement.

So, we go through the elements of $U$ and check if they are in $S,$ as follows. Remember that we are looking for elements that are *not* in $S.$

- For the element $1 \in U,$ we have $1 \not \in S. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- For the element $3 \in U,$ we have $3 \not \in S. \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

- For the element $5 \in U,$ we have $5 \in S. \quad \color{red}\times$

We found that the elements $1,3,4$ are in $U$ but not $S.$

Therefore, the complement of $S$ is

$$
\overline{S} = \{ 1,3,4 \}.

$$
f(-x) = f(x).
$$

The graph of an even function is always symmetric about the $y$-axis.

![](images/fc/fc57d05c6bef23243df97979c0680054c6ec66b836a97871970ee055c60eab4a.png)

Also recall that $g(x)$ is an **odd function** if

$$
g(-x) = -g(x).
$$

17592186045417] [17592186046673 1008 "This course introduces students to proof-writing essentials, bridging the gap between pure problem-solving and constructing formal mathematical arguments. Students will formalize their understanding of logic, sets, and functions while delving into new concepts such as congruence, relations, and cardinality.
This course serves as ideal preparation for students wishing to pursue undergraduate studies in formal mathematical disciplines, including Discrete Mathematics, Abstract Algebra, and Real Analysis.
The prerequisite for Methods of Proof is single-variable calculus, which would be satisfied by completion of either Calculus II, AP Calculus BC, or Mathematical Foundations III." 17592186045417] [17592186046673 1009 "Students begin by mastering the basics of logic and logical operations, including statements, predicates, connectives, logical laws, logical equivalence, conditional and biconditional statements, quantifiers, inference, and formal and informal language. By solidifying their grasp of these logical fundamentals, students will have a secure underpinning that enables them to embark on their journey into proof-writing confidently.
A robust knowledge of set theory is another cornerstone of mathematical proof-writing. Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.
After mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts
This challenging yet engaging course helps students with strong mathematical foundations build a solid base for further progression into advanced undergraduate courses." 17592186045417] "Interesting mathematical problems often involve a large (or infinite) collection of sets. Labeling each set with a subscript is often convenient in such situations. 

For example, suppose we define a collection of sets $A_i$ for $i\in\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N$ as follows:

$$
A_1 = \{1,2\}, \qquad A_2 = \{3,4\}, \qquad A_3 = \{5,6\}, \qquad \ldots
$$

Note the following:

- This collection of $A_i$'s, which we denote $\big\{ A_i \big\}_{i \in \mathbb N},$ is called a **family of indexed sets.**

- The set $i=\{1,2,3,\ldots\} = \mathbb N$ is called the **index set**.

Writing each set with a subscript makes talking about a general $A_i$ easier. In this particular case, for example, we can express a general member of this family in terms of its index:

$$
A_i = \{2i-1,\, 2i\}, \qquad i\in\mathbb N
$$

So, if we wanted to write down the elements of $A_{100},$ we substitute $i=100$ into the definition of $A_i{:}$

$$
A_{100} = \big\{2(100)-1,\, 2(100)\big\} = \{199,200\}
$$

We can use any index set when defining a family of indexed sets. 

For example, consider the indexed family $\big\{ B_x \big\}_{x \in \mathbb R},$ where $B_x$ is the real interval defined by

$$
B_x = \big[ 0, x^2 \big), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

Here, the index set is $\mathbb{R}.$ 

To write down, say, the elements of $B_{\color{blue}\sqrt{5}},$ we substitute $x={\color{blue}\sqrt{5}}$ into our definition of $B_x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}_{\sqrt{5}} & =[0,\,(\sqrt{5})^{2}) \\  & =[0,5)\end{aligned}

![](images/6e/6e38185922e9cad6d3961e7c5e755eabf4c52eafd1cc81a1e81a383b4df5ae82.png)

To get this second-degree Taylor polynomial, we add a second term to the linear approximation:

$$
P_2(x) =  \underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}_{\text{linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{new quadratic term}}.
$$

As it turns out, we can keep on adding more and more terms, each time getting better and better approximations. The **third-degree Taylor polynomial** approximation to $f(x),$ denoted $P_3(x),$ is given by

$$
P_3(x) =  \underbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \dfrac{1}{2!}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\text{quadratic approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{3!}f^{(3)}(a)(x-a)^3}_{\text{new cubic term}}.
$$

Note that $f^{(3)}$ represents the third derivative of $f.$ In other words, $f^{(3)} = f'''.$

In general, $P_3(x)$ is a better approximation to $f(x)$ compared to $P_2(x),$ provided that $x$ is close to $a.$

- The first-degree Taylor polynomial is the linear approximation.

The starting point of the vector projection is $O,$ and the ending point will be the point $P$ that lies on the line containing $\mathbf{b}$ with $AP \perp \mathbf{b},$ as shown below.

The vector $\overrightarrow{OP}$ is called the **vector projection** of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$ It is denoted as $\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a},$ and it is computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =OP\cdot u \\  & ={\text{comp}}_{b}\,a\cdot u\end{aligned}
$$

where $\text{comp}_{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{a} = |\,\mathbf{a}\,| \cos\theta$ is the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{b}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =|\,a\,|\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}

$$
\mathbf{u} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{|\,\mathbf{b}\,|} = \dfrac{\mathbf{b}}{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \mathbf{b}

$$
